Review Date: Reviewed in the United States on December 1, 2024
Review Body:
The hillbilly identity always resonated with me, even though I personally grew up on the edge of the culture. Or perhaps, I just thought our way of life was normal. JD's descriptions seem to fit my grandparents generation more than my own (I'm now 69 years old) but the drinking, infidelities, coal mining jobs, distrust of government, church attendance, and personal values of honor, family loyalty, and pride ring true to me. Each of my maternal grandparents came from families of 18 children; they had 9 children including my mum. Grandma Genny was pregnant with her last child (stillborn) at the same time my mum was pregnant with her fourth child (out of five).

Grandpap owned his own "house mine" for a while to earn a living. He often filled neighbors' empty coal bins without getting paid, but he did it anyway because he didn't want kids to be cold. You looked out for each other.

None of my aunts or uncles went to college. My mum, the 3rd oldest, was the first to graduate from high school - even though she got pregnant, married in April, and took her husband to the prom. Her principal had seen her marriage license in the paper and greeted her on the following Monday by telling her that he "hoped this didn't affect her school attendance".

I guess I AM a 3rd generation hillbilly! Fortunately, people in my life guided me; my mum's proud that I was the first grandchild to graduate from college. I'm grateful to have been a teacher for 35 years, teaching children in West Virginia and Western PA - educating my kind of people. I loved them!

Review Date: Reviewed in the United States on March 22, 2020
Review Body:
Most of the readers of J.D. Vance’s excellent autobiography, “Hillbilly Elegy,” will probably have little to no interaction with the large sub-culture of Americans from Appalachia. In fact, the elite readers who only read NYT best-sellers have likely scorned these people as white trash or, as they have been called in politics, “deplorables.” But Vance’s book illustrates the strong family values and the honor in hillbilly communities through his life story. On the other hand, he also shares the dark side and admits that the hillbillies need to dig themselves out of some very destructive habits.
Vance touches on an important point about income mobility in the United States. Many people believe the myth that there is little economic mobility in America, that it’s hard for a poor person to ever escape poverty. If you look at government statistics, though, you’ll see that’s not really true. The hillbilly population seems to have a greater mobility problem than other poor communities, but hillbillies are the exception, not the rule. According to a U.S. Treasury Study, “Income Mobility in the U.S. from 1996 to 2005,” “There was considerable income mobility of individuals in the U.S. economy during the 1996 through 2005 period as over half of taxpayers moved to a different income quintile over this period. • Roughly half of taxpayers who began in the bottom income quintile in 1996 moved up to a higher income group by 2005. • Among those with the very highest incomes in 1996 – the top 1/100 of 1 percent – only 25 percent remained in this group in 2005. Moreover, the median real income of these taxpayers declined over this period.” In other words, according to the Treasury study, folks at the bottom moved up and those at the top dropped. Vance cites a Harvard study by Ram Chetty (and others) that examines why the hillbillies don’t have the same mobility as other Americans with similar finances. But Vance goes further to point out that he didn’t need the academic paper to show him that the causes are “the prevalence of single parents and income segregation.” [Income segregation is the physical separation of various peoples by class based on income. For example, certain people cannot get into country clubs because of insufficient funds.] He goes on to explain that the government welfare and social services don’t really understand the culture and therefore cannot actually help. It’s the same old problem of government bureaucrats from far away trying to impose their values on local communities instead of assisting those communities to find their own solutions. Just throwing money at a problem, like giving welfare checks that keep people forever dependent on the government, perpetuates a problem from generation to generation.
Vance shows how the government interference fails on many levels. For example, when talking about how the government sometimes removes a child from his or her family, Vance writes, “Part of the problem is how state laws define the family. For families like mine—and for many black and Hispanic families—grandparents, cousins, aunts, and uncles play an outsize role. Child services often cut them out of the picture, as they did in my case. Some states require occupational licensing for foster parents—just like nurses and doctors— even when the would-be foster parent is a grandmother or another close family member. In other words, our country’s social services weren’t made for hillbilly families, and they often make a bad problem worse.” When I read that sentence, I was reminded of a great book, “Bottleneckers: Gaming the Government for Power and Private Profit,” by William Mellor and Dick M. Carpenter II, which explains the problems when the government requires licensing. In “Bottleneckers,” the authors do not mention the issue that Vance does about how licensure can stop an extended family member from caring for a child, but that would be another great point for them to make.
With so many five star reviews of J.D. Vance’s book, adding mine to the fray may not influence someone to read the book. But I do hope that if you’ve read this review, you will then read “Hillbilly Elegy” with an eye towards seeing how the government has failed so many poor people, not just hillbillies.

Review Date: Reviewed in the United States on April 20, 2019
Review Body: I'm thankful my Adverse Childhood Experiences score is 0. Some hillbillies take heat when they move; not being from their new home, they are different. Dwight Yoakam of Kentucky sang that they learned "Readin' Rightin' Route 23." One of the jokes was taking Route 23 North would lead to luxury and comfort. The joke would be your mom's such a hillbilly her false teeth have cavities. The author writes: Why did poor kids struggle in school? His teacher said parents wanted them to be shepherds to their kids, but no one wants to talk about the fact that many are raised by wolves. People ask him what he'd like to change about the white working middle class. He answers the feeling that our choices don't matter. The Marine Corps excised that feeling in him "like a surgeon does a tumor." He once had a professor say his paper was "a vomit of sentences masquerading as a paragraph. Fix." At Yale Law, he felt his spaceship had crashed in Oz, but he got in! His wife hadn't learned how to fight in the hillbilly school of hard knocks. There was no drama at Thanksgiving. Her mother didn't complain about her father behind his back while his mom had a revolving door of boyfriends. There were no suggestions that family friends were liars or backstabbers. In France, the percentage of children exposed to three or more maternal partners is .5 percent. In the U.S., it's 8.2 percent. For many kids, the impulse is to escape, but they rarely choose the right door. His salutatorian mom had a baby and divorce, but not a single college credit before her teen years were over. She had given birth and buried a child before she could drive. It's out of the frying pan and into the fire. Chaos begets chaos. Instability begets instability. Welcome to the family life of the American hillbilly. They need mentors to learn self-preservation. They are on guard all the time.

Review Date: Reviewed in the United States on January 10, 2018
Review Body:
ance uses his life story and that of his family and extended family in order to explain the cultural and economical ways of the hillbilly. Just what is a hillbilly? Generally, they are someone who is from the Appalachian Mountain region who is poor, rural, and working class. Sometimes undereducated. The stereotype has them with no teeth because they drink Moutain Dew and don't go to the dentist. Also that they are gun happy people ready to use them especially if you get their daughter pregnant. The heavy popping of opioid pills such as Percocet and Oxy began in the mountains of West Virginia and Kentucky, which is where the term "pillbilly" comes from.

Vance's Mamaw and Pawpaw came from a holler in Kentucky called Jackson. He got her pregnant at the age of thirteen and the two took the famous Route 23 out of Kentucky to Ohio (sometimes referred to as "Middletucky") where a good job at a steel manufacturer, Amaco, awaited. They weren't the only ones. Plenty of people from Appalachia left for jobs in Michigan, Indiana, Pennsylvania (or "Pennsyltucky"), and Illinois. In the 1950s thirteen out of one hundred in Kentucky took the hillbilly highway out and in Harlan County Kentucky, thirty percent of its population, mostly coal miners, left.

Life was hard for his Mamaw and Pawpaw. She had several miscarriages and three children that survived. These included Uncle Jimmy, Aunt Wee, and his mother. His Pawpaw was an alcoholic and things could get ugly in their house. He would straighten himself out and while he and his wife stayed married they would end up with their own separate homes once their kids were grown, but remained close. But heaven help anyone who bothered one of the children or a member of the family. When Uncle Jimmy was five, he saw a toy in the pharmacy that he wanted for Christmas and his parents told him to go in and look at it while they finished shopping at a store. When he picked it up to play with it, the clerk in the store told him that he wasn't allowed to touch the toy and kicked the boy out of the pharmacy. When his parents found him and found out what happened they went in and trashed the place and stood up for their son's honor, because how dare someone tell their son that he can't come in their store.

He would take a while to adjust to a new place as his mother moved him and his older sister, Lydnsey, around to different homes with different men. The one constant was his Mamaw's place. Life with his mother was hard as she had a temper and in her relationships, fighting was the only way she knew how to deal with things. So dishes went flying and she would get violent with the men in her life.

According to J.D., this was how most hillbillies acted. Also, they spent money they didn't have at Christmas on fancy gifts for the kids, hoping the IRS refund check would cover it. Sometimes there would be someone in the house with a substance abuse problem. In J.D.'s case, it was his mother who got hooked on pills. They also abuse the Welfare system and try to get out of work if they can.

Vance basically says that you have to pull yourself up by your bootstraps, but most of these people don't have boots. And he had helped himself. His Mamaw received a pension check from his Papaw when he died and likely social security. He credits his Mamaw, his sister, his teachers, and the Marines with helping him to avoid going down the wrong path and instead earning his degree at Ohio State and his law degree at Yale, something practically unheard of from where he was from. He offers a lot of criticism but no solutions and he overgeneralizes and forgets the people in his life that weren't loud and violent like his sister and Uncle Jimmy and Aunt Wee and cousin Gail and their spouses. It's like he wants them to be the exception that proves the rule, but there are more of them in his life than the violent argumentative types. Also, I think there are plenty of people who are dying to get jobs of any kind if you just give them a chance. And there are programs that train people in Appalachia to learn a new trade for a company that is in the area. Vance is close to using stereotypes, though with stereotypes there is some truth to them. Read this book with caution.

*Vance is contemplating a run for office and it is my opinion that he wrote this book as a stepping stone for this purpose. But that is just my opinion.

* I add this as I think it might be interesting and be a counterpoint to the book.

I was born in poverty in Appalachia. ‘Hillbilly Elegy’ doesn’t speak for me.

J.D. Vance, author of “Hillbilly Elegy,” in Washington in January. (Astrid Riecken/For The Washington Post)

By Betsy Rader September 1, 2017

Betsy Rader is an employment lawyer at Betsy Rader Law LLC, located in Chagrin Falls, Ohio. She is running as a Democrat to represent Ohio’s 14th Congressional District in the U.S. House.

J.D. Vance’s book “Hillbilly Elegy,” published last year, has been assigned to students and book clubs across the country. Pundits continue to cite it as though the author speaks for all of us who grew up in poverty. But Vance doesn’t speak for me, nor do I believe that he speaks for the vast majority of the working poor.

From a quick glance at my résumé, you might think me an older, female version of Vance. I was born in Appalachia in the 1960s and grew up in the small city of Newark, Ohio. When I was 9, my parents divorced. My mom became a single mother of four, with only a high school education and little work experience. Life was tough; the five of us lived on $6,000 a year.

Like Vance, I attended Ohio State University on scholarship, working nights and weekends. I graduated at the top of my class and, again like Vance, attended Yale Law School on a financial-need scholarship. Today, I represent people who’ve been fired illegally from their jobs. And now that I’m running for Congress in Northeast Ohio, I speak often with folks who are trying hard but not making much money.

Although high school graduation rates are rising and there are more private and federal grants available, most low-income students have a tough time attending and staying in college. Here are nine facts about poor students and the college experience. (Video: Claritza Jimenez/Photo: iStock/The Washington Post)

A self-described conservative, Vance largely concludes that his family and peers are trapped in poverty due to their own poor choices and negative attitudes. But I take great exception when he makes statements such as: “We spend our way into the poorhouse. We buy giant TVs and iPads. Our children wear nice clothes thanks to high-interest credit cards and payday loans. We purchase homes we don’t need, refinance them for more spending money, and declare bankruptcy. . . . Thrift is inimical to our being.”

Who is this “we” of whom he speaks? Vance’s statements don’t describe the family in which I grew up, and thy don’t describe the families I meet who are struggling to make it in America today. I know that my family lived on $6,000 per year because as children, we sat down with pen and paper to help find a way for us to live on that amount. My mom couldn’t even qualify for a credit card, much less live on credit. She bought our clothes at discount stores.

Thrift was not inimical to our being; it was the very essence of our being.

With lines like “We choose not to work when we should be looking for jobs,” Vance’s sweeping stereotypes are shark bait for conservative policymakers. They feed into the mythology that the undeserving poor make bad choices and are to blame for their own poverty, so taxpayer money should not be wasted on programs to help lift people out of poverty. Now these inaccurate and dangerous generalizations have been made required college reading.

Here is the simple fact: Most poor people work. Seventy-eight percent of families on Medicaid include a household member who is working. People work hard in necessary and important jobs that often don’t pay them enough to live on. For instance, child-care workers earn an average of $22,930 per year, and home health aides average $23,600. (Indeed, it is a sad irony that crucial jobs around caretaking and children have always paid very little.)

The problem with living in constant economic insecurity is not a lack of thrift, it is that people in these circumstances are always focused on the current crisis. They can’t plan for the future because they have so much to deal with in the present. And the future seems so bleak that it feels futile to sacrifice for it. What does motivate most people is the belief that the future can be better and that we have a realistic opportunity to achieve it. But sometimes that takes help.

Yes, I worked hard, but I didn’t just pull myself up by my bootstraps. And neither did Vance. The truth is that people helped us out: My public school’s guidance counselor encouraged me to go to college. The government helped us out: I received scholarships and subsidized federal loans to help pay my educational expenses. The list of helpers goes on.

Now that so many people have read “Hillbilly Elegy” this summer, I hope they draw this better moral from the story: Individuals can make a difference in others’ lives, and by providing opportunities for all, our government can do the same. Life, liberty and the pursuit of happiness should be legitimate expectations for everyone, “hillbillies” included.

Review Body: First off, Middletown, Ohio which is in Butler County and in the SOUTHWESTERN part of Ohio, is not even in Appalachia. This author may be talking about Kentucky, but the picture on the front of his book is somewhat confusing and is nothing like Middlwtown, Ohio which is a little less than 30 square miles and has an average altitude is 600 feet. It is not mountainous although there are some hills and valleys. I'm from Middletown, was born and raised there, and my life was not privileged (very middle class)in any respect, but nor was it ANYTHING like the authors. He paints a picture of a town that is foreign in my opinion to the reality. Ok.....maybe he did it to sell books, but this is not a non fiction account. Obviously most is fiction or seen from an entirely different perspective than I experienced or saw growing up there. I resent my hometown being portrayed as a whole in this light and referred to as part of Appalachia or as the title indicates, 'hillbilly'. Totally inaccurate. Doesn't anyone question the authenticity of statements such as this before believing factless conclusions? My family was blue collar, hardworking in the steel mill and paper mill, not abusive, never on welfare, never unemployed, never on drugs. I got a full college scholarship based on need and academics. First one in my family to attend college. We were conservative, patriotic ( my uncles and Father all served in military), church going, loyal, and honest. We lived in a post war subdivision in a small home, but our house was clean, maintained, and all my siblings and I were taught respect for others. We were not racists, bigots, or any other slanderous type label. We, and many others that I met from my childhood to my teenage years, were just plain average, warm hearted, hard working Americans from Middletown, Ohio, which was coincidently named an All American City in 1957. Middletown families and individuals did not exhibit the jaded fault finding traits as concluded and seemingly described overall by the author. I, and many other Middletonians would take exception to his generalized portrayals. He should speak only of his personal upbringing and dysfunctional family issues and not blame the town environment for his own woes and experiences.

Review Date: Reviewed in the United States on August 7, 2017
Review Body:
This was an interesting read for me...I'm from the deep South so I know certain elements of this well. I'm a Scotch-Irish descendant, so I know that well. My family spent years in Ohio...so I've been exposed to that. So I feel pretty well qualified to distinguish between "southern" "poor" "hillbilly" "Scotch-Irish", etc.

I think J.D. did an interesting job of putting story to paper, I'm just not so certain that his assumptions and conclusions are well-formed. From the silly (I'm not from Kentucky, but I sure do call my Mamaw "Mamaw", so if he didn't know one before, there it is...and I'm not alone...GA, AL, TN, MS ...we all say it) to the profound. J.D., don't spend any more time telling me your assessment of why the Hillbilly's don't like Mr. Obama - You ARE Mr. Obama...well, you're white, but the parallels of your lives are unmistakable to anyone except you. Abandoned by the father, raised by a single Mom...important presence of the Grandparents...brief forays into not-too-terrible misbehavior...bright mind...college on scholarships...I wished he had explored these similarities and really looked at why he was "OK" but Mr. Obama was vilified by these folks. Made me realize that JD is a bit too young to interpret much of this...

All that said, a valuable read...a bit tedious in places The language and the violence..startling. This is not about place...so much as class...poor people who are frustrated (frustration breeds aggression, and all that...)...and about blame and anger and, yes, about survival...about the ability to come out the other side. Not too many characters I'd like to know, but amazing that both he and his Sister beat the odds.

Review Date: Reviewed in the United States on July 22, 2017
Review Body:
I write this review while relaxing underneath a shade tree among the Eastern Kentucky hills of Wolfe County. Just minutes previous, I finished reading "Hillbilly Elegy." Before purchasing the book, I read all of the preview and quickly realized that the life of J.D. Vance closely paralleled mine in numerous ways. I had to read this book!

Our life's similarities are staggering. We both had Eastern Kentucky roots: his family hailed from Breathitt County while mine was firmly planted in neighboring Wolfe County. J.D.'s grandparents moved north to Middletown to find work and a better life. My mother, step-father, and I also moved to Middletown, Ohio for supposedly the same purpose. Mom didn't go through men like Vance's, but I eventually dealt with two step-fathers. J.D.'s father was virtually absent as was mine. We both had grandparents that served as caregivers and primary role models during various points in our lives. J.D. graduated from Middletown High School and joined the marines (spelled purposely without capitalization to emulate the spelling in the book). I graduated from nearby Lemon-Monroe High School and joined the United States Marine Corps (Semper Fidelis!). Without delving into any turbulence in the households while growing up, our parallels pretty much end there.

With all that said, I was mindfully prepared to relate to and bond with J.D. Vance's story. Despite my best efforts, I could not get to that point. How could I have so much in common with the author and not connect with them on a personal and an emotional level? I'll tell you how. The book wasn't written for me and the thousands of other "hillbillies" that experienced the migrations north. The book was obviously written and edited as fodder for an academic crowd because it reads primarily like a white paper. The infinite colons and semicolons really stand in the way of an emotional connection. In my opinion, Vance's story would have been much better for a mainstream audience if it had been written less formally.

If you have never been part of an exodus from Appalachia, this book may be for you. You may find J.D.'s story intriguing, shocking, and possibly a catalyst for further study. For those of us that were forced to leave our hollers, you'll probably be reading and thinking, "Just suck it up and get on with your life." I really don't mean to sound harsh, but we must make the best out of the cards that life deals us. (You will always lean on crutches until you throw them away.) Of course, you can always write a book. (For years, I have debated writing a similar book.)

Maybe part of my disconnect with "Hillbilly Elegy" is because I migrated to Ohio directly while J.D.'s family was already rooted in Middletown at his birth. Another reason may be a generational gap. My stint in Middletown occurred in the 1970's, over a decade before J.D.'s birth. (I was serving in the United States Marine Corps when he was born in 1984.)

Regardless, I wish J.D. Vance and his Ohio and Kentucky families the best.

Review Date: Reviewed in the United States on July 13, 2017
Review Body:
Hillbilly Elegy: A Memoir of a Family and Culture in Crisis by J.D. Vance (Harper Collins, 2016, $12.59/15.99) has been on the NY Times Best Seller List for forty-nine weeks, and at the time of this writing, stands at number two. This touching, revealing, warm, sad, and inspiring memoir, written by a Yale Law School graduate whose childhood was spent in the hills of eastern Kentucky and the migrated community of Middletown, OH, opens many sores while explaining in the most human and personal terms possible the pain and misunderstanding that harms working class and poor white Americans in the Hheartlands. Throughout this tale Vance sometimes mentions findings of academic studies and other research, using them to support or introduce his own poignant experiences, but, most of all, this is the story of one man's ability to persevere in an environment where success such as he has experienced is rare, and , according to him psychically costly as well as economically expensive.

Living within a home with serial father figures coming and going and an alcoholic, drug addicted mother, he attributes the source of his core values to life in rural Jackson, Kentucky in the hills and hollers of Appalachia with his Mamaw and any number of uncles and cousins. He describes on academic paper in which the authors suggest that “hillbillies learn from an early age to deal with uncomfortable truths by avoiding them, or by pretending better truths exist, a characteristic of bluegrass music, too. Vance refuses to look the others way.

Vance tracks the two major migrations from Appalachia to the industrial mid-west, particularly Middletown, OH, which were mirrored in the South, mid-South and New England, the depression era migrations and the post-WWII migration of returning veterans. He examines how the regions prospered and then died off with the decline of America industrial might, leaving abandoned neighborhoods, unemployment, and drug dependency behind, attributing this to both bad government policies and globalism.

Vance consistently refers to himself and his family as being poor and then at other times being “working class.” Joan C. Williams, in White Working Class seems to make a clear distinction between the two while Vance vacillates. He talks about “his people,” Kentucky migrants to southern Ohio, as often living off the dole, not working, and being plagued by drugs and violence, yet also talks about an uncle who escapes to the middle class, and his mother who, despite being an addict, was a nurse who was able to work a good deal of the time. He glories, however, in his extended family, his many uncles who provide him with male role models in both positive and negative ways. At times he seems remarkably judgmental, while at others, forgiving.

As Vance matures through adolescence, he begins to see the disjointures between both liberal and conservative points of view. He sees many of the government programs as well meaning but ineffective while the conservative solutions were disciplinary and draconian. In his reading of sociology, while in high school, he began to realize that the situation of black people described in his readings about black America contained the same dilemmas as did the lives and existence of the white working poor from Appalachia. “Our Elegy is a sociological one, yes, but it is also about psychology and community and culture and faith.” (144) He's writing about religion, work, and family when he observes the deep “cognitive dissonance between the world we see and the values we preach.” (147)

As Vance prepares to attend Yale Law School he explains in touching, no-holds-barred language why a person like him, growing up in poverty, bedeviled by the rigors of having a drug addicted mother living with multiple husbands, and seemingly inured to violence and loss could reject the attractions of both the left and the right. These chapters, presented within the context of an actual life lived in poverty and difficulty, if not despair, bring so many working class and poor white men, especially, to accept so much patently untrue or misleading material in seeking to understand who they are, why they got that way, and how difficult it is to extricate oneself. In short, Vance asserts, it's easier for many to blame “the other” than it is to do the hard analysis of one's own choices, accept the verdict, and get to work to change things. What sets J.D. Vance apart is his ongoing optimism, despite all evidence to the contrary.

Interestingly, Hillbilly Elegy can also stand as a “How To” book for those seeking to find their own way to a different place in both the workplace and in society. For instance, the non-verbal behavioral cues of social class are significantly different than the behaviors that pass for progressing in working class employment and social environments. Vance shows himself always to be exceptionally alert to what's going on around him. As he gains in self confidence, his ability to ask questions of those he trusts increases. He's also a very fast learner. Nevertheless he owns to deep feelings of abandoning the culture from which he comes while yearning to become part of that with which he's not, yet, thoroughly familiar. However, the struggle is neither easy nor always successful.

Throughout Hillbilly Elegy: A Memoir of a Family and Culture in Crisis, Vance scatters data and information from relevant sociological and psychological writing to illuminate the points he makes, to give them a solid theoretical context. Such use of accurate research information never seems intrusive or fault-finding. Rather, it seeks to help a reader generalize from the highly personal revelation of the pain and confusion of Vance's childhood. It helps the reader gain understanding and perspective without ever excusing either those who raised him or his own mis-understandings, missed paths, and possibly botched relationships. He bravely opens the scars on his psyche, examines them, faces their consequences, and comes out the other side a stronger and better person. His painstaking honesty with the reader and his courage are never in doubt. This is not a book for the reader to quarrel with. Rather, it requires being good listeners, seeking to find the truths as they apply to them. Some would prescribe better, more effective programs. Others view the problems of poverty and drug addiction as the fault of the victim. While, ultimately, Vance looks towards personal responsibility for life, he fully understands the necessity for a compassionate government and individual acceptance of responsibility working together to make progress possible for all. I bought the book and read it on my Kindle app.

Review Date: Reviewed in the United States on June 23, 2017
Review Body:
I hated this book, and it has nothing to do with my political beliefs, etc. It reads like a poorly written term paper that is desperately in need of a good editor. There is nothing groundbreaking about this book, and I didn't learn anything other than Mr. Vance should thank his lucky stars that somehow someone somewhere had enough influence to convince everyone in America they needed to read this. His writing is basic at best, he seems to be able to judge everyone harshly except those in his own family, he contradicts himself and doesn't give good arguments to back his opinions, and is arrogant to boot.
I can read anything if it is engaging and thought provoking, but this was the longest 272 pages of my life.

Review Date: Reviewed in the United States on February 22, 2017
Review Body:
Reads like a sophomore term paper: "What I did on my summer vacation (with my redneck extended family)". Not very well written and of absolutely no interest except to document what it's like to live in a dysfunctional family. The author's primary (albeit unsupported) conclusions: all families from Appalachia are similarly dysfunctional. All members of dysfunctional families experience bad lives and dashed hopes.

Bah. Cannot fathom the multitude of 5-star reviews. Avoid.

Review Date: Reviewed in the United States on February 16, 2017
Review Body: first hand account of an essentially permanent white underclass, which rates as suddenly an interesting question in light of the recent presidential election. interesting read, lots of anecdotal evidence, without being political. some lightweight supporting notes, but it isn't trying to be a research paper.

Review Date: Reviewed in the United States on January 12, 2017
Review Body:
First, I come from an extremely poor family (years without indoor plumbing, eating chicken food casseroles (as in casseroles made from cheap chicken feed really), newspaper for toilet paper, etc.) So I get the poor and disadvantaged angle for real.

Second, I currently am close to two family dynasties similar to that described in this book, one from Tennessee, the other generations here in Michigan. Both with a strong sense of family but much conflict; almost zero emphasis on education, almost zero expectation of personal success.

So I think I get it but it's complicated. On the one hand, the author seems to go to great lengths to both romanticise and praise the "toughness" (IE, bullying and mindless machoism) of his hillbilly roots, while waving away the racism, bigotry and close-mindedness of that culture. As well as spending - I thought - a wee bit too much time defending and rationalising his views and sympathy for hillbilly culture, which he admits is bigoted, violent, anti-intellectual, racist, misogynistic...indeed, willfully ignorant. Which is the worst kind of ignorance, I think. It's a refusal to accept new information and progress (define that as you will.)

On the other hand, he sketches out some guidelines for moving forward and is emphatic in his praise for those people in his life who fostered higher goals.

I'm also impressed that, at a fairly young age, he was able to write such a cogent memoir. I'd be interested to read a follow-up in 20 or 30 years.

Review Date: Reviewed in the United States on January 8, 2017
Review Body:
I found Hillbilly Elegy (Kindle Version) an interesting and engaging read. It brings one face-to-face with the struggles of that around 13% of the population that live in poverty and the many more who live near the poverty line. While it focuses on the experiences of the descendants of the immigrants who populated Appalachia and, later, the rust belt, the takeaways can be extrapolated to the larger swath of America that faces economic struggles. The author touches on quantitative and qualitative reasons for this populations’ particular struggle with economic mobility, with the main themes being a loss in confidence in the American Dream, failed familial relationships, and lack of exposure to the possibilities that are reserved for the upper and upper-middle class. This book is a particularly topical given the recent election and focus on the growing inequality in America.

What made this work better than an economic paper on the rise of inequality is the author’s personal experience with the struggles that are faced by a large swath of our society. I found this aspect of the book the most appealing. The author credits idiosyncratic reasons for his ability to escape this environment. He does not give many policy prescriptions for the treatment of ills that plague his community, nor does he portend to, but he does lay much blame at the feet of his community. While I have similar political leanings to the author, his prognosis seems inconsistent with his own experiences. Claiming he made it out by sheer luck and supportive grandparents, it is unclear how he would have done this under different circumstances through hard work, which he claims is a lost value in his community. This is underscored other places in the memoir where he claims ignorance in the ways of the upper class, such as etiquette and networking. The latter, he says, is the most important way to make it ahead. I also did find it unusual that while he diagnoses these problems, he did not describe becoming significantly involved in any effort to be that example of success that his community so sorely lacked.

Review Date: Reviewed in the United States on January 7, 2017
Review Body: A deeply insightful look beyond the headlines into the cultural issues that are too often overlooked. The loss of meaningful blue collar work, widespread government assistance programs, meth and painkiller epidemics - this book takes us firsthand into the lives, histories, and programs that got us here. If only the solutions could be as succinctly put on paper. Congratulations to J.D. Vance for an important, revealing - and ultimately, what must have been a painful to write - book.

Review Date: Reviewed in the United States on January 3, 2017
Review Body: Well written insight into a segment of the population that's not typically visible to coastal America. I like the fact that it doesn't paper over the complexities of the struggles of the "hillbillies" and the challenges of helping this large group of people.

Review Date: Reviewed in the United States on December 8, 2016
Review Body: This is a great book - very insightful. Certainly well worth the read. I didn't know what Rust Belt was until the election and then had only occasionally heard reference to it. The media seemed to indicate that region had made the difference in the presidential outcome. After reading this book, I learned a great deal about that area of the U. S. and its "culture" as Vance refers to it. And then in this morning's paper, George Will drew attention to it saying "...his [Vance's] book is often misread as primarily about the toll taken by economic forces - globalization, automation, etc..."; however, I agree with Will that the book really illustrates the learned helplessness and other cultural factors involved in many individual and family lives. The author is in a good position to know as he grew up in the culture described in the book. The situation can be applied to many poverty areas in the U. S. This is a must read!

Review Date: Reviewed in the United States on December 6, 2016
Review Body:
I read this book -- well, most of it -- knowing that Vance was a Trump apologist and that he worked for Peter Thiel, the famous Trump mega-donor who believes that the 2008 bank collapse was caused by poor people. So I wasn't surprised by Vance's poverty-shaming philosophy. Rather, I looked forward to gaining some insight into what life in America's hollers was about. And, after all, the book had received glowing reviews, and not just from conservatives.

What I found, sadly, was a book that used a few anecdotes about hillbilly life in its early chapters to justify what was, overall, just a screed that repeated shopworn talking points blaming poor people and drug addicts for being...well, poor people and drug addicts. Every now and then, Vance either cherry picks or misrepresents an academic paper to support his philosophy, which is basically that poor folk should be more like him. Work harder. Blame your mother, not your poverty. Join the military, because it'll get you into shape. (Like most bleeding heart liberals, I prefer working out at the Y to basic training and war, but cut me some slack; my own family history doesn't support the notion that respect for authority will make America great again.)

In short: Libertarians 1, Readers 0. The title is not just deceptive but cynically misleading. There are no insights here, just a poorly written rehash of predatory, libertarian philosophy. It's not an elegy; it's a screed, and a rehashed one to boot. There might be a National Review column in this, but this relentlessly self-congratulatory and repetitive monograph was a fraud that left me poorer for having spent the time and money on it. If you want to understand poverty, a little Dickens goes a lot farther than what seemed like an awful lot of Vance. There's nothing new here. Pandering to the right and suckering the left might be a great business model, but elegiac it ain't.

Review Date: Reviewed in the United States on September 22, 2016
Review Body: Part term paper, part autobiography, Vance's story confirms what I've discovered about my family and my youth. You only know what you know. If those who raise you are flawed, it is likely that you will embrace those flaws and make them your own. Only by stroke of luck or sheer determination will you find someone who opens your eyes and shows you the exit. And when you look back at your life and think, "how did I not see that [bigotry] [stupidity] [wrong path]," you realize how different your life would be if you had stayed, and how lucky you are to have escaped. The government, with intent to "help," has done permanent damage to its most vulnerable citizens. If you feed the animals in the wild, they will stop looking for food and are not likely to become self-sustaining again. Vance is right; the government can't fix this problem. And those enmeshed in it most often don't even know or want to know the way out. A fascinating, sometimes depressing read.

Review Date: Reviewed in the United States on September 16, 2016
Review Body:
J.D. Vance’s A Hillbilly Elegy is a memoir or a telling of his memories of childhood in Middletown, Ohio, and Kentucky. This memoir is well worth reading and giving a great deal of thought to today. Vance’s family were the products of Appalachian culture in Kentucky. We called them “Hillbillies” or “Briar Hoppers.” They were migrants recruited to work in the steel mills, paper mills, and factories of the once prosperous industrial Midwest. They did dangerous, boring, and physically fatiguing work well and cheaply. Like all immigrants, they came looking for a better life, but brought their culture with them.

When oppressed, discriminated against, and ridiculed, it was this culture they instinctively turned to in order to redress the wrong they continued to endure both from external society and from their own culture adrift in a different environment.

In Vance’s childhood, the decline of the rust belt economy had started. A drive down Middletown’s First Avenue or Central Avenue today will convince you that the decline is virtually complete. If you are modern, educated, and thoroughly middle class, you’ll see living anthropology or sociology. If you are from there, and have escaped or migrated elsewhere yourself, you may be overcome by sorrow.

Understanding Appalachian culture is very difficult to do because it is beset by popular stereotype. The settlers of the Appalachia in the 18th and 19th Centuries were lowland Scots, displaced Irish, German, Welch and others who were as a group Yeoman farmers. The bloody Kentucky we’ve read about was about wresting the land from the Native American and economic and political struggles between the landed agrarian society of Virginia and also indigenous competition for wealth and influence. The fact that these migrants lived in isolation and were originally yeomen farmers let their original culture perpetuate itself for generation after generation. Yes, you can still hear Elizabethan speech in their dialect. More importantly, this culture defined the roles and expectations of men and women. A man was to provide for his family. A woman was to maintain life in the home and nurture children. To fail at either cost you your place in this society. In a culture tainted by the expectation of misery and a life that whose only antidote is endurance, drugs, alcohol, and abuse are a common result.

Understanding this gives you an appreciation for the dysfunctional family life, fighting, and substance abuse Vance saw and had to cope with as a child. It’s little wonder he turned to living Appalachian icons of self-sufficiency, endurance, and rebellion to sustain himself. How could you turn to the law to protect yourself when the law evicted you, was bought off, and was a tool of oppression?

You need to know that the sons and daughters of these hillbillies went on to better jobs, educated themselves, and prepared their own sons and daughters to succeed. You also need to know that the poverty and isolation of Appalachia still exists and perpetuates itself in cities like Middletown.

I hate to leave you with a totally negative impression. There is fantastic beauty in Appalachian culture.

Review Date: Reviewed in the United States on September 6, 2016
Review Body: Is it that any book about Americans seen as "different" gets ecstatic critical reviews? This work is poorly organized, repetitious, contradictory, and above all generically and poorly written. Lots of summary and broad statements. Very little of the precise detail that makes a memoir compelling. Sentences like "my heart raced with excitement" and "I finally understood what made her tick" abound. Periodically -- randomly, jarringly -- the throws in some study or academic paper to buttress a point. With skilled editing, what J.D. Vance has to say might have made a compelling long essay. But here: filler, filler, filler. Boring, boring, boring. I almost never give up on a book, but I couldn't finish this one. What a disappointment.

Review Date: Reviewed in the United States on August 21, 2016
Review Body: Congratulations to J.D. Vance for overcoming some truly appalling childhood circumstances. As a memoir, the book is a compelling personal tale of triumph set against a portrait of a region helpless to help itself. I grew up in a rural area a few miles outside of Middletown and my father was from Jackson Ky, so when I heard about this book, I simply had to read it. In age, I am contemporary with Mr. Vance's mother, and the area was suffering economically when I left Ohio for good, well over 30 years ago. The book is at its strongest in relating personal history and reactions--this is a very inspiring journey. It falls very short in its attempts to be illuminate larger truths without the scholarship or broader insights it would take to support such message. And at times it seems like that message is a self-proclaimed hillbilly giving the hometown lazy Lil Abner mattress testers the much needed kick in the drop seat of their straw covered union suits he thinks they so richly deserve. It purports to have special insight into the 'hillbilly' culture. Beyond relating the (obviously exaggerated) colorful exploits of Mamaw's family and some sort of peculiar pop-culture inspired of tales of blood feuds fought by the coarse-mouthed and belligerent, this book is exclusively rooted in greater Middletown. Middletown is so generically described it could be any blue collar region anywhere in the country that has lost its economic engine, leading to entrenched systemic poverty and the ills that go with it. The sad outcomes of those who migrate from rural poverty to urban poverty is a universal story: as true in Lima, Peru as in Lima, OH. Given the title, one might have expected to learn more about the 'briar hoppers' who migrated to the factories away from the land that had shaped many of those families who settled on Frozen Creek more than 200 years ago. As a note, I can not recall ever hearing anyone from Breathitt County refer to themselves as a hillbilly. As for being the 'ah ha' book that explains current political climate, it's too mired in a self-serving worldview to accomplish much. The Middletown portrayed by Vance is an echo chamber of ignorance, hopelessness and despair, and while I haven't looked up the statistics, it seems as if the drug culture has gotten significantly worse. Yes, it's like that: I well remember anger as the default emotion and the ease with which it can stoked to reaction. I remember the sweeping condemnations of people desperate to be better than someone, anyone. And it saddened me to see that Mr. Vance has yet to leave those attitudes behind, and worse, uses them to justify heap scorn on a region that has been punished more than enough. Mr. Vance has a very selective understanding of "the thumb on the scale". Vance's ticket out of Middletown was a long standing US Government funded institution--the Marines. Public assistance puts money in to the community, enabling a grocer to employ a teenaged cashier fortunate enough to have a strong work ethic and ambition to better his circumstances. For someone determined to turn over the rocks of his hometown, the treatment of racism and xenophobia was curiously tepid and understated. The implication that Ohio legislators are out-of-touch do-gooders for trying to limit predation on the poor because they don't understand how convenient payday loans can be was simply astonishing. Vance didn't go to OU right out of high school because he couldn't figure out the financial aid form? Really? This Marine Corp Veteran with a public affairs background is so intolerant of the views of others that he rushes to complete his college degree? Honestly? The post high-school part of the book didn't really add up. Highly successful people from and in the Miami Valley are not as rare as hen's teeth, as Mr. Vance so often implies. Vance is a very young man, still raw with the traumas of his childhood. The most genuine parts of this memoir reveal a man struggling with his pain and searching for peace and an idenity and the ability to forgive the parents who failed him. I wish him well in that, and wish that his time at Yale had taught him the value of critical thought.

Review Body: I knew a family like this through marriage. The effects of drugs plus the family toxicity created havoc. The only grownups in the room were the grandmother and the child. The book gave me a better understanding of the difficulty of breaking away and that government programs are nice on paper but do not translate into anticipated results.
